concepts.gloss: The grammatical status usually marked by dependent function or by distinct subordinate form, not equivalent in every instance to being a dependent.
The status of a head clause within a containing construction, even when a different clause also appears in the sentence.
Internal syntactic cues to subordination, including a subordinator, a relative gap, or open-interrogative phrase placement and subject–predicator order.
A content clause licensed as a complement yet internally identical in form to a main declarative clause.
A subordinate-marked clause in an elliptical answer or rare independent exclamatory construction with no governing predicate.
A wh-relative clause functioning as a supplement rather than an integrated dependent, despite its subordinate syntax.
A dependent clause that preserves main interrogative inversion in a restricted construction, with the complete distribution deferred to §5.3.1.
A subordinate content clause with a subjunctive plain-form verb classified as finite rather than infinitival.

rules.concept: subordination versus main clause head function
rules.statement: A subordinate clause characteristically functions as a dependent of another construction, while a main clause can be the head of that construction even when it contains other clauses.
rules.condition: When assigning a clause's structural status within a larger construction, distinguish a clause functioning as modifier or complement from the head clause; do not classify a clause as subordinate merely because it occurs inside a sentence that contains another clause.

contrast.text: The article Mira recommended is unavailable. [relative clause modifies article]
Theo believes that Mira is correct. [that-clause is complement of believes]
Although the report was lengthy, it was helpful. [although heads an adjunct PP; it was helpful is the main/head clause]
The revised report was helpful. [one main clause without subordination]

rules.review_notes: The source says 'characteristically', not invariably: standalone subordinate-form clauses and supplementary relatives are counterexamples to an absolute dependent-only definition (CLS-068). Owner-approved; no independent second pass.

rules.concept: structural marking of subordinate clause form
rules.statement: Subordinate clause form can be signalled by an introductory subordinator, an understood gap, or the combination of an initial interrogative phrase with subject-before-predicator order.
rules.condition: For a subordinate clause, inspect overt structural cues separately: that before a declarative content clause, a relative construction with a missing understood object, or a subordinate open interrogative with a prenuclear interrogative phrase and uninverted subject–predicator order.

contrast.text: It seems clear that Lea made an error. [subordinator that]
The documents Ben submitted were complete. [relative with an understood object gap]
They asked which route Farah would take. [subordinate open interrogative: subject Farah before auxiliary would]
Which route would Farah take? [corresponding main open interrogative with inversion]

rules.review_notes: These are examples of internal marking, not exhaustive necessary conditions: unmarked dependent content clauses are also possible (CLS-067). Source p. 949.

rules.statement: A finite declarative content clause may function as a subordinate complement even when no part of its internal structure distinguishes it from an independent main clause.
rules.condition: When a finite declarative clause is licensed as a complement of a matrix predicate, recognise subordination from its syntactic function even when there is no that marker or other internal cue; whether that can be omitted in a particular construction is addressed separately in Chapter 11 §3.1.

contrast.text: I know the printer is broken. [bare subordinate content-clause complement]
The printer is broken. [the same internal words as an independent main clause]
They said the rehearsal had ended. [bare subordinate content-clause complement]
They said that the rehearsal had ended. [marked counterpart]

rules.review_notes: The existence of bare content clauses does not mean every subordinate declarative can omit that. Specific obligatory and excluded environments are deferred by the source to Ch. 11 §3.1.

rules.statement: A clause with subordinate structural marking need not actually be a dependent: elliptical answers, rare independent exclamatory content clauses, and supplementary relative clauses can retain subordinate form without dependent function.
rules.condition: When analysing a structurally subordinate-form clause used as an independent elliptical response, as an independent exclamatory construction, or as a supplementary relative, distinguish its internal subordination marker from whether it is a syntactic dependent in a larger construction.

contrast.text: A: What did the committee request? B: That the schedule be revised. [independent elliptical answer with that]
That everything should end in such confusion! [rare independent exclamatory content clause]
Nora phoned her old mentor, who now lives nearby. [supplementary relative, not an integrated dependent]
Nora phoned the mentor who lives nearby. [integrated relative functioning as NP modifier]

rules.concept: main-clause form in a dependent clause function
rules.statement: A clause functioning as a dependent may sometimes retain main-clause interrogative structure, including subject–auxiliary inversion, instead of exhibiting the usual subordinate interrogative order.
rules.condition: In the specified predicate-complement pattern exemplified on p. 950, recognise that an interrogative with main-clause inversion can function as a dependent; do not generalise the distribution to all embedded interrogatives, which normally retain subject–predicator order.

contrast.text: The real question is why did nobody notify the staff? [main interrogative form in complement function]
The real question is why nobody notified the staff. [ordinary subordinate interrogative form]
They wondered why nobody notified the staff. [normal subordinate interrogative with no inversion]
